title: The Gas Bank: from a Missouri chicken truck to the largest bankruptcy in America
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Tyrone, Missouri: the second child
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Birth date, parents Omer and Ruth (Rees) Lay, and the Tyrone birthplace are given by the Texas State Historical Association Handbook of Texas entry 'Lay, Kenneth Lee' and corroborated by Wikipedia. Coordinates corrected during verification: Tyrone, Missouri sits at 37.20333, -91.87667 per the Wikipedia infobox; an earlier working figure of 37.4756, -91.7346 was roughly thirty-two kilometres off and has been discarded.
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of April a second child is born to Omer Lay and Ruth Rees Lay in Tyrone, an unincorporated scatter of houses in the southern hills of Texas County, Missouri. Omer sells farm equipment and stoves and whatever else will move, and preaches on Sundays as a Baptist lay minister. The family goes where the work is, which is nowhere for long. Tyrone has no bank and no exchange and no market of any kind that a boy could study. They name him Kenneth Lee.
suggested_refs: The Handbook of Texas entry on Kenneth Lee Lay, which records the birth and the family's poverty in consecutive lines
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Lay, Kenneth Lee'

stops.name: Rural Missouri: the truck and the chickens
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The failed chicken venture and the truck accident are carried by the Texas State Historical Association biography as paraphrased in the research dossier and could not be independently confirmed against a primary account. No source reached gives a year; 1949 is an ordering device inside Lay's childhood and carries no evidentiary weight. Placed at the Tyrone pin because no source names the road or the county the accident happened in.
stops.campa: Omer Lay puts what the family has into chickens and hauls them toward market. The truck is wrecked on the road and the birds are lost. There is no insurance and no second try. The son who watches this will spend his working life inside an industry that never touches what it sells, buying and selling natural gas by contract along pipe owned by other men. Nothing he trades will ride in the back of a truck he owns. The venture closes the way the earlier ventures closed, and the family goes where the next work is.
suggested_refs: The family-story episodes in the Handbook of Texas biography, none of them documented from a primary source
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Lay, Kenneth Lee'

stops.name: Columbia, Missouri: the family stops moving
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the fact of the relocation, by the Texas State Historical Association Handbook of Texas, which dates it only to the 1950s. The year 1955 is chosen to order the segment and is not given by any source reached; neither the month nor the exact year is recoverable. The boyhood jobs are carried by the same reference work and by Wikipedia.
stops.campa: The Lays stop moving. They settle in Columbia, a university town in the middle of Missouri, and the boy takes the work a boy takes there: paper routes, lawns, a tractor on a farm outside town. He is in his teens, and the family has no money to send anyone to the university whose economics faculty will take him in on scholarship inside the decade. The campus of the state university stands at the far end of Providence Road from the house, and the tuition on it is money the Lays do not have.
suggested_refs: Columbia, Missouri, the university town where the itinerant years ended
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Lay, Kenneth Lee'

stops.name: David H. Hickman High School, Columbia: the diploma
stops.date_confidence: Graduation year attested by the Texas State Historical Association Handbook of Texas; the month and day are not given anywhere reached and June is a convention. The extracurricular detail rests on a kewpie.net alumni page cited in the dossier, which was not independently refetched, and on Wikipedia. Coordinates corrected during verification: Hickman High School, 1104 N Providence Road, is at 38.96333, -92.33139 per the Wikipedia infobox.
stops.campa: He graduates from David H. Hickman High School, the public high school of a college town. The alumni record keeps the plain list: band, choral groups, the National Honor Society, student office. It is the record of a boy who did everything asked of him and nothing that startled anyone. His father is still preaching and selling, his mother keeps the house, and there is no tuition money in the family. Scholarship money is waiting at the university two miles down Providence Road. He is eighteen.
suggested_refs: The Hickman High School alumni record for the class of 1960
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Lay, Kenneth Lee'

stops.name: University of Missouri, Columbia: Pinkney Walker's student
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The B.A. in economics (1964) and the M.A. (1965) under Pinkney Walker are given by the Texas State Historical Association Handbook of Texas and by Wikipedia; the Phi Beta Kappa election and the Beta Theta Pi chapter presidency come from the same institutional biographies. Neither degree is dated to a month. The pin is the main campus at Jesse Hall.
stops.campa: On scholarship he reads economics under Pinkney Walker, who will matter to the rest of his life more than any employer does. Walker is a working economist with Washington connections, and he will pull his student after him twice: first into a federal commission, then toward the industry that commission regulates. Here the teaching and the patronage are the same thing, and they are never separated afterward. Lay is elected president of his Beta Theta Pi chapter and taken into Phi Beta Kappa. He takes the bachelor's degree in 1964 and stays for the master's, finished the following year.
suggested_refs: Pinkney Walker's economics seminars at the University of Missouri, 1960 to 1965
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Lay, Kenneth Lee'

segments.name: Houston, the Pentagon, and the Dissertation

stops.name: Humble Building, Houston: corporate economist
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Employment at Humble Oil and Refining from 1965 to 1968 is given by Wikipedia and the Texas State Historical Association; the month of hire is not recorded anywhere reached. The building is identified as Humble Oil's 1963 to 1973 headquarters at 800 Bell Street; Lay's own office within it is undocumented. Coordinates corrected during verification: 800 Bell Street geocodes to 29.75359, -95.36956.
stops.campa: His first employer is Humble Oil and Refining, the Texas company that will be folded into Exxon, and his first title is corporate economist. The Humble Building on Bell Street is forty-four stories of new downtown Houston, and the work inside it is forecasting: what crude will cost, what the refineries will run, what demand does next. He is twenty-three, holds two degrees in a discipline the company uses as an instrument, and is living in the city he will run a corporation out of twenty years later. He stays three years.
suggested_refs: The Humble Building at 800 Bell Street, Houston, headquarters of Humble Oil 1963 to 1973
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Lay, Kenneth Lee'

stops.name: The Pentagon, Arlington: the Navy Comptroller's man
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to service dates (1968 to 1971), the rank of lieutenant, the January 1968 entry into Officer Candidate School, and the Navy Commendation and National Defense Service medals, per Wikipedia and the Texas State Historical Association. A contradiction is flagged and not resolved: the research dossier described the posting as financial and economic analyst in the Office of the Assistant Secretary of the Navy, while the Wikipedia article it cites says 'special assistant to the Navy Comptroller.' The campa follows Wikipedia's wording.
stops.campa: He enters Navy Officer Candidate School in January and is commissioned. The war in Vietnam is at its height and he spends it in Arlington, at a desk, working the money as special assistant to the Navy Comptroller. The building he reports to each morning buys more of everything than any other institution on earth, and the timing of that buying becomes his subject, first in uniform and then in print. He rises to lieutenant. He leaves the Navy in 1971 with the Navy Commendation Medal and the National Defense Service Medal.
suggested_refs: The Office of the Comptroller of the Navy, the Pentagon, 1968 to 1971
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Lay, Kenneth Lee'

stops.name: University of Houston: the Vietnam buildup
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The University of Houston institutional repository record (uh-ir.tdl.org, author Kenneth Lee Lay, 1970) gives the year and the full title. A correction is recorded: the commonly quoted title 'An Analysis of the Vietnam Buildup' is only the subtitle. No month is given; June is a convention. The absence of any later book or memoir is a negative finding, checked and stated as a gap.
stops.campa: The University of Houston grants him the doctorate for a dissertation on defense procurement, titled The measurement of the timing of the economic impact of defense procurement activity: An analysis of the Vietnam buildup. He is writing, a few miles from the refineries, about the lag between the order a government places and the money reaching the economy that fills it. It is the only sole-authored scholarly work of his life. There is no memoir afterward, and no book of any kind, and nothing else in the record with his name alone on it.
suggested_refs: Kenneth Lee Lay, doctoral dissertation, University of Houston, 1970, in the UH institutional repository
sources: University of Houston institutional repository, uh-ir.tdl.org

stops.name: Federal Power Commission, Washington: technical assistant
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the post and the patron by the Texas State Historical Association and Wikipedia; the year 1971 is given, the month is not. Placement is city-level only: the Federal Power Commission's exact street address in 1971 and 1972 was not confirmed within the research budget, and the coordinates should be read as downtown Washington, not as a building.
stops.campa: Pinkney Walker is a commissioner of the Federal Power Commission now, the agency that fixes the price at which interstate pipelines may sell natural gas, and he brings his former student in as technical assistant. The wellhead price ceilings the commission enforces are producing exactly the shortages their opponents predicted, and Lay reads the files on them from the desk that writes them. The industry those files govern is the one he will work in for the next thirty years. He is twenty-eight years old.
suggested_refs: The Federal Power Commission's wellhead price ceilings, the regulatory regime Lay learned from the inside
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Lay, Kenneth Lee'

stops.name: Department of the Interior, Washington: Deputy Undersecretary for Energy
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the appointment, by the Texas State Historical Association and Wikipedia. The departure year is contradicted and not resolved here: the Handbook of Texas and a family obituary give different years (1973 against 1974), and Wikipedia says only 'until 1974.' No month is recorded for either end of the post. Coordinates are the Main Interior Building at 1849 C Street NW.
stops.campa: Nixon's Interior Department makes him Deputy Undersecretary for Energy. He is thirty years old and holds a federal energy post in the years the American energy order breaks apart. He argues for letting price find its own level; two administrations later that will be the argument of the entire industry, and he will be making it from inside. The shortages arrive on schedule. Gas is curtailed to the factories through the winter, and then the embargo comes and the lines form at the pumps.
suggested_refs: The Main Interior Building, 1849 C Street NW, Washington
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Lay, Kenneth Lee'

stops.name: George Washington University, Foggy Bottom: the last teaching
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and a source problem is flagged rather than resolved. The graduate teaching at George Washington University appears in the research dossier's geography lens attributed to the Wikipedia article 'Kenneth Lay,' but a refetch of that article found no mention of George Washington University at all. No substitute source carrying the detail was located within the research budget, so the claim stands unsourced. The date is an ordering device inside his Washington years.
stops.campa: While he holds the Interior post he teaches graduate courses in economics and in the relations of government and business at George Washington University, a mile and a half up the street from his office. He is thirty-one and has been in Washington three years. It is the last teaching he ever does. Twenty-six years afterward he will pay for a chair in economics at his own alma mater rather than occupy one anywhere. Why he stopped is not stated in anything that survives.
suggested_refs: The Foggy Bottom campus of George Washington University, a mile and a half from the Interior Department
sources: Research dossier chronology, attribution to Wikipedia not confirmed on refetch

stops.name: Winter Park, Florida: the other side of the desk
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the move to Florida Gas Transmission within the Continental Group, by Wikipedia and the Texas State Historical Association; the year is given variously as 1973 or 1974 and is not resolved here. Coordinates are the centre of Winter Park; the specific office building was not identified in any source reached.
stops.campa: He leaves Washington for Florida and the other side of the desk: Florida Gas Transmission, a pipeline company inside the Continental Group, in the suburban quiet of Winter Park outside Orlando. He is thirty-two, a regulator become an operator, responsible for the first time for steel in the ground rather than for the rules about it. The line runs from the Texas fields across the Gulf states to the peninsula. The whole business of it is moving other men's gas under contract, and charging them for the passage.
suggested_refs: The Florida Gas Transmission line, from the Texas fields to the peninsula
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Lay, Kenneth Lee'

stops.name: Winter Park: the first chief executive's office
stops.date_confidence: Contradicted and left contradicted. The Texas State Historical Association makes him president and chief executive of Florida Gas by 1980; Wikipedia says he was 'president of Continental Resources from 1981 to 1982,' a different corporation inside the same structure and neither the same title nor the same year. The dossier's original claim merged the two into one sentence that neither source supports. The date here follows the earlier of the two accounts as a segment-ordering choice only.
stops.campa: Six years after he arrives he is running the company. Florida is the end of the pipe, the market of last resort, a peninsula with no gas of its own and a growing population that needs it. The economist who read price ceilings at the Federal Power Commission now sets tariffs against them, hires and fires, and answers to a board. From here the ladder goes toward bigger systems and bigger companies, and in the direction of Houston. Whether the title is Florida Gas or Continental Resources, and whether he is thirty-eight or thirty-nine when he takes it, the sources do not agree.
suggested_refs: The corporate structure of the Continental Group, in which Florida Gas and Continental Resources are distinct entities
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Lay, Kenneth Lee'

stops.name: Transco Energy, Houston: back to Texas
stops.date_confidence: Date contested and not resolved. The Texas State Historical Association puts the move to Houston as president of Transco in 1981; Wikipedia's career sequence puts Continental Resources at 1981 to 1982 and the Transco posts running only 'until 1984,' implying a 1982 start. No source reached gives a month, and an earlier claim of May 1981 is unsupported. Coordinates are Transco Tower (now Williams Tower) at 2800 Post Oak Boulevard, 29.7372, -95.4614; note the tower did not open until 1983 and cannot be the venue for any earlier part of the tenure.
stops.campa: He comes back to Houston at forty as president and chief operating officer of Transco Energy, and joins its board. Transco owns the great interstate line running out of the Gulf toward New York. The deregulating gas market of the early eighties has begun to reward whoever will buy at one price and sell at another rather than merely charge for the passage, and Lay has never worked anywhere except inside that market or above it. Transco's own tower on Post Oak Boulevard will not open until 1983.
suggested_refs: Transco Tower, 2800 Post Oak Boulevard, Houston, completed 1983
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Lay, Kenneth Lee'

stops.name: Houston Natural Gas, downtown Houston: chairman at forty-two
stops.date_confidence: The appointment as chairman and chief executive of Houston Natural Gas in June 1984 is attested by the Texas State Historical Association. The takeover pressure from Irwin Jacobs is carried by a single secondary account and is tagged as reconstruction. The exact street address of the HNG headquarters was not confirmed in anything reached; the pin is a generic downtown Houston point and should not be read as a building.
stops.campa: Houston Natural Gas, under takeover pressure from the raider Irwin Jacobs, makes him chairman and chief executive in June. He is forty-two. His answer to a raider is size: buy pipeline, sell whatever is not pipeline, make the company too large and too coherent to be swallowed. The board gives him the office and the free hand together. Within a year he has bought lines reaching both coasts, and the company that hired him to keep it from being merged is about to merge.
suggested_refs: The 1984 takeover pressure on Houston Natural Gas from Irwin Jacobs
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Lay, Kenneth Lee'

stops.name: InterNorth headquarters, Omaha: the merger announced
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia's merger chronology, corroborated by company material cited in the dossier; the merger became effective in July. Coordinates are InterNorth's historic Omaha headquarters building. No source found places Lay personally in that building on that date, and the negotiations may have happened elsewhere; the pin marks the counterparty, not an attested presence.
stops.campa: On the second of May, Houston Natural Gas and InterNorth of Omaha announce that they will merge. InterNorth is the larger company and owns the Northern Natural system across the plains; Houston Natural Gas is the smaller and supplies the chief executive. The merged corporation is to keep its headquarters in Nebraska. It does not. Within a year the head office is in Houston and the Omaha men are gone. Omaha keeps the building and loses the company.
suggested_refs: The Northern Natural Gas Building, Omaha, headquarters of InterNorth

stops.name: 1400 Smith Street, Houston: the company is named Enron
stops.date_confidence: Attested that the merged HNG and InterNorth company took the name Enron with Lay as chairman and chief executive, per Wikipedia and the Texas State Historical Association. Sources place the renaming across 1985 and 1986, with February 1986 given for the start of the chairmanship; the January date here is a segment-ordering convention. Coordinates corrected during verification: 1400 Smith Street is at 29.7556, -95.3719 per the Wikipedia building article. The tower was formerly Four Allen Center.
stops.campa: The merged company takes the name Enron, and Lay takes the chairmanship and the chief executive's office at 1400 Smith Street, a tower that had been called Four Allen Center. He is forty-three and runs the largest interstate natural gas system in the United States, assembled inside two years out of two companies, neither of which he founded and neither of which was his. The name is new and means nothing yet. He holds the chairmanship from here until January 2002, and the office at 1400 Smith Street for as long.
suggested_refs: 1400 Smith Street, Houston, formerly Four Allen Center, the Enron headquarters tower
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Lay, Kenneth Lee'

stops.name: Valhalla, New York: the traders and the offshore accounts
stops.date_confidence: The scandal itself is attested: the unauthorized trading and falsified records at Enron Oil, and the later criminal convictions of Louis Borget and Thomas Mastroeni, are documented in standard Enron corporate history. No source establishes that Lay personally visited the Valhalla office. The quotation attributed to him, that he told the traders to keep making the company millions, is explicitly unverified in the dossier and was not located in any contemporaneous transcript; it is described in the campa as unlocated and is not asserted as fact. No month is recorded.
stops.campa: In a suburban office north of New York City, two men running Enron's oil trading arm, Louis Borget and Thomas Mastroeni, move money through offshore accounts, falsify records, and trade far beyond their limits. The company loses heavily and both are prosecuted. Nineteen years later the affair comes back into a Houston courtroom as evidence on the question of what the chairman knew in 1987. The line everyone repeats, that he told them to keep making the company millions, has never been found in any transcript.
stops.quote: Rules are important, but they should not—you should not be a slave to rules, either.
stops.quote_source: Kenneth Lay, criminal trial testimony under cross-examination by John Hueston, 2006, Famous Trials archive (transcript reproduces the dash)
suggested_refs: The criminal proceedings against Louis Borget and Thomas Mastroeni over Enron Oil
sources: Research dossier account of the Enron Oil proceedings

stops.name: 1400 Smith Street, Houston: Skilling and the gas bank
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the year and the role: Jeffrey Skilling, formerly of McKinsey, joined Enron in 1990 to lead Enron Finance Corporation and developed the gas bank model, per Wikipedia and standard Enron corporate history. No month is recorded anywhere reached.
stops.campa: A McKinsey consultant named Jeffrey Skilling comes over to run Enron Finance and brings the idea the company will be rebuilt on: the gas bank, in which Enron stands between producer and buyer and sells not gas but the certainty of its price. Enron buys forward from producers who need cash, sells forward to utilities who need a fixed number, and takes the spread. The pipes stay in the ground and stop being the point of owning them. In sixteen years the two men will be tried together on one indictment, in a courtroom a few blocks from this office. Lay hires him and keeps him eleven years.
suggested_refs: Enron Finance Corporation and the gas bank model, 1990

stops.name: Rice University, Houston: co-chair of the economic summit
stops.date_confidence: Attested, and upgraded during verification. The co-chairmanship was originally carried only by Enron's own archived executive biography and tagged as reconstruction; CBS News, 'Bush Edges Away From Kenny Boy' (8 July 2004), independently reports that 'Lay served as co-chairman of the former President Bush's economic summit for industrialized nations held in Houston that year.' The coordinates match Wikipedia's for Rice University, which hosted the 1990 G7 Houston Economic Summit. Only the month is fixed; the day is a convention.
stops.campa: The Group of Seven meets in Houston in July, hosted by George H. W. Bush in his adopted city, and Lay serves as a co-chairman of the summit. It is the highest station he has yet stood in and it is not a business station at all: the chief executive of a four-year-old gas company at the shoulder of the president of the United States while seven governments talk about oil and debt. The president's son, a Texan in the oil business himself, already calls him Kenny Boy.
suggested_refs: The 1990 Houston Economic Summit of industrialized nations, hosted at Rice University
sources: CBS News, 'Bush Edges Away From Kenny Boy,' 8 July 2004

stops.name: Astrodome, Houston: the convention comes to his city
stops.date_confidence: The convention itself is attested: Wikipedia gives the 1992 Republican National Convention as running 17 to 20 August 1992 at the Astrodome. Lay's role as a leading host-committee figure is a reconstruction: it rests on the dossier's characterization of contemporaneous reporting and on the CBS News 'Kenny Boy' piece, and is not mentioned in the Wikipedia article on the convention. Coordinates are inherited byte-identical from the atlas's existing Astrodome pin in george_hw_bush.journey.json, which is 29.6847, -95.4107; a geocoded value of 29.6850, -95.4078 was set aside to keep the pin consistent across files.
stops.campa: The Republican National Convention comes to the Astrodome for four days in August, and George H. W. Bush is renominated in the building where the Astros play. Lay stands at the head of the Houston host committee: the local money, the local welcome, the man who brings the party to town. Enron is by now the largest natural gas company in the country, and its chairman has made himself the civic face of a city that runs on the industry he leads. In November the president loses.
suggested_refs: The 1992 Republican National Convention, Astrodome, Houston, 17 to 20 August
sources: CBS News, 'Bush Edges Away From Kenny Boy,' 8 July 2004

stops.name: Dabhol, Ratnagiri district: the plant on the plateau
stops.date_confidence: The plant, its location, its capacity of 2,015 megawatts, the twenty-year contract with the Maharashtra State Electricity Board, and Enron's role are attested by Wikipedia's article on the Dabhol Power Station. The dispute is documented as running to 2001. No source reviewed establishes that Lay personally visited the site; his own dealings on Dabhol are attested in Delhi and Washington, not here. The date orders the segment at the project's beginning and is not a documented day.
stops.campa: On a coastal plateau in Ratnagiri district, a hundred miles south of Bombay, Enron begins the largest and most contested thing it will ever build: a power station of two thousand and fifteen megawatts, under a twenty year contract with the Maharashtra State Electricity Board. The dispute over its cost and its terms will run nine years, through cancellation, renegotiation, arbitration and protest at the gates, and the state that signed the contract will spend the decade trying to get out of it.
suggested_refs: The Dabhol Power Station at Anjanwel, Ratnagiri district, Maharashtra

stops.name: University of Missouri, Columbia: the endowed chair
stops.date_confidence: Attested, with a source correction recorded. The gift of roughly 1.1 million dollars in Enron stock in 1999 and the September 2005 request to redirect the endowment to Hurricane Katrina relief are carried by The NonProfit Times, 'Even In Death Lay's Gift Stirs Controversy'; the KRCG-TV article originally cited for the amount carries neither the figure nor the year, and supplies instead Joseph Haslag, 2008, and the 'career suicide' email. The chair is in international economics. No month is given for the 1999 gift.
stops.campa: He gives the University of Missouri about one million one hundred thousand dollars in Enron stock, and the university endows a chair in international economics with his name on it. Thirty-four years earlier he had walked that quadrangle on somebody else's scholarship. The name stays on the chair. In September 2005, indicted and waiting for trial, he asks the university to redirect the endowment to Hurricane Katrina relief; the chancellor recommends granting the request, and the leadership declines it.
suggested_refs: The Kenneth Lay Chair of International Economics, University of Missouri, held by Joseph Haslag since 2008
sources: The NonProfit Times, 'Even In Death Lay's Gift Stirs Controversy'
KRCG-TV, 'Enron's legacy looms 20 years on at University of Missouri'

stops.name: 1400 Smith Street, Houston: EnronOnline opens
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day: Wikipedia's Enron article gives EnronOnline's launch as 29 November 1999, with Enron generally acting as counterparty. The revenue figure of nearly 101 billion dollars and net income of 979 million dollars are the as-filed fiscal year 2000 numbers, later restated after the collapse; they are given here as filed and not as an audited later truth. The quotation is from Lay's letter to SEC chairman Arthur Levitt of 20 September 2000, and so postdates this stop by ten months.
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of November the company opens EnronOnline, a trading screen on which Enron is itself the counterparty to nearly every transaction that crosses it. The gap between what a book like that turns over and what it earns is the whole business model, and almost nobody outside the building reads it as a warning. Within a year the company reports revenue of nearly one hundred and one billion dollars against net income of nine hundred and seventy-nine million. Those are the figures as filed, before the restatements.
stops.quote: Enron has found its 'integrated audit' arrangement to be more efficient and cost-effective than the more traditional roles of separate internal and external auditing functions.
stops.quote_source: Kenneth Lay, letter to SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt, 20 September 2000, reproduced on PBS Frontline
suggested_refs: EnronOnline, launched 29 November 1999
Enron's fiscal year 2000 annual report, as filed
sources: PBS Frontline, Lay letter to Arthur Levitt

stops.name: 1400 Smith Street, Houston: the letter to Arthur Levitt
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. The letter is reproduced in full on PBS Frontline. The quotation is given in its corrected form: the source text reads 'I also respectfully urge,' and an earlier transcription dropped the word 'also.' The pin is Enron's Houston headquarters, from which Lay wrote; the letter was addressed to the Securities and Exchange Commission in Washington.
stops.campa: The Securities and Exchange Commission proposes to limit the non-audit work an accounting firm may sell to a company it audits. Lay writes to the chairman, Arthur Levitt, in defense of the arrangement Enron keeps with Arthur Andersen: an integrated audit, with the internal and external functions in one firm's hands. Fifteen months later Andersen's Houston office is shredding Enron documents by the cartload. Enron has found the arrangement, the letter says, more efficient and more cost-effective than the more traditional roles of separate internal and external auditing functions.
stops.quote: I also respectfully urge the Commission to reassess the need for such broad regulatory intervention when the business environment is more dynamic than ever.
stops.quote_source: Kenneth Lay, letter to SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt, 20 September 2000, reproduced on PBS Frontline
suggested_refs: The September 2000 SEC auditor-independence rulemaking and the comment letters filed against it

stops.name: 1400 Smith Street, Houston: Skilling takes the office
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the month by Wikipedia: Skilling became chief executive of Enron in February 2001 while Lay remained chairman; no day is given, and the first of the month is a convention. Skilling's 1997 elevation to president and chief operating officer is separately attested.
stops.campa: Skilling takes the chief executive's office and Lay keeps the chairmanship, the succession the company has been arranged around since 1997. Lay is fifty-eight and has run something without interruption for twenty years. The trading floor is the company now and the pipelines are its ballast. Formally he is chairman and not manager, and his lawyers will build a defense on that distinction five years from now. What a chairman is supposed to have known is a question the courtroom will put and the record still does not settle.
suggested_refs: Enron's 1997 succession arrangement, under which Skilling became president and chief operating officer

stops.name: The White House complex, Washington: half an hour with the Vice President
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to detail, attested as to fact. The meeting with Vice President Dick Cheney on 17 April 2001 during the energy task force process is carried by contemporaneous Washington Post reporting as characterized in the dossier, and is corroborated by the broader GAO and NRDC litigation record over the task force's visitor logs; it was not independently refetched. The room within the complex is not established. The 100,000 dollar inaugural donation is independently confirmed via CBS News.
stops.campa: He meets the Vice President for about half an hour inside the White House complex while the administration's energy task force is being assembled, and argues for market pricing and for opening the transmission grid to whoever will pay to use it. He and his wife gave one hundred thousand dollars to the inauguration in January. George W. Bush has called him Kenny Boy for a decade, and eight months from this meeting nobody in this building will take his call. Which room in the complex the half hour was spent in has never been put on any record released to the public.
suggested_refs: The GAO and NRDC litigation over the 2001 energy task force visitor records
sources: Washington Post reporting on the Cheney energy task force, as cited in the research dossier
CBS News, 'Bush Edges Away From Kenny Boy,' 8 July 2004

stops.name: New Delhi: the appeal over Dabhol
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The July 2001 trip to India and the September 2001 letter to Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee are carried by the dossier chronology alone and were not independently refetched against a primary contemporaneous account. The dossier does not name the Indian city the July trip involved; New Delhi is an assumption made to give the stop a pin, and the coordinates are the city, not a building. The World Bank's refusal to back the project is reported in the interlock lens as a known part of the record.
stops.campa: He goes to India himself over Dabhol. The contract is in open collapse, the state electricity board has stopped paying, and the plant is shut. The World Bank has already refused to finance the project's later phase. He is fifty-nine, four months from the bankruptcy of his own company, and he has flown halfway around the world to argue about one power station. In September he writes to Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee asking for a settlement. No answer that reaches him in time is on the record.
suggested_refs: Lay's September 2001 letter to Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee on the Dabhol dispute
sources: Research dossier chronology, not independently refetched

stops.name: 1400 Smith Street, Houston: Skilling resigns and Lay returns
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia: Skilling resigned unexpectedly on 14 August 2001 citing personal reasons, and Lay resumed the chief executive role while remaining chairman.
stops.campa: Six months into the job Skilling resigns for personal reasons and gives no explanation the market believes. The board hands the chief executive's office back to Lay the same day. He is fifty-nine and has been chairman without operating command since February; now he has both again, and the company he gets back is not the one he handed over. Everything that follows is dated from this day. The letter arrives tomorrow morning and the employee meeting is the morning after that. Fourteen weeks remain between this day and the bankruptcy filing.
suggested_refs: Skilling's resignation statement of 14 August 2001

stops.name: 1400 Smith Street, Houston: the Watkins memorandum
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to substance, dated only to the month. Sherron Watkins's warning letter to Lay and its phrase about imploding in a wave of accounting scandals are well established in the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations record and in the trial evidence; the verified pool fixes it to August 2001 without a day, and 15 August is chosen only to sit between the resignation and the employee meeting. The location of the subsequent face-to-face meeting is inferred to be the Houston headquarters and is not independently documented.
stops.campa: An Enron vice president named Sherron Watkins writes the chairman an anonymous memorandum about the Raptor structures, the off-balance-sheet vehicles hedging Enron's own investments with Enron's own stock. Then she meets him face to face and puts her name to it. She is not the first person inside the building to see what the structures are. She is the one who writes it down and hands it up the stairs. The company, the memorandum tells him, could implode in a wave of accounting scandals.
stops.quote: implode in a wave of accounting scandals
stops.quote_source: Sherron Watkins, letter to Kenneth Lay, August 2001, as recorded in the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations record
suggested_refs: The Watkins letter as printed in the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations record
sources: Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations record, as characterized in the research dossier

stops.name: 1400 Smith Street, Houston: Lay It on the Line
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to venue and form. The 16 August employee address and the later companywide online forum called Lay It on the Line are part of the well-established trial record, sourced in the dossier to the Justice Department's Enron trial-exhibit archive, which returned a 403 error on refetch and could not be read directly. The forum is dated by the dossier to September 2001; the 16 August date here is the employee address. The quotation is Lay's own, from the trial transcript excerpt published by the Famous Trials archive.
stops.campa: The morning after the letter he stands in front of the employees and tells them the company is sound. In September he holds a companywide online forum called Lay It on the Line, and answers questions about a stock that has lost most of its value since January, from people whose retirement accounts are made of it. The exchanges are kept, printed, and put in front of a jury four and a half years later. His personal belief, he tells them, is that Enron stock is an incredible bargain at current prices.
stops.quote: My personal belief is that Enron stock is an incredible bargain at current prices, and we will look back a couple of years from now and see the great opportunity that we currently have.
stops.quote_source: Kenneth Lay, criminal trial testimony, United States v. Lay and Skilling, transcript excerpt, Famous Trials archive
suggested_refs: The Justice Department's archived Enron trial exhibits, justice.gov/archive/index-enron.html
sources: Research dossier citation of the DOJ exhibit archive, refetch blocked

stops.name: 1400 Smith Street, Houston: the October announcement
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by the standard Enron collapse chronology and Wikipedia: on 16 October 2001 Enron announced a large quarterly loss and major charges, together with a reduction in shareholder equity tied to related-party transactions. The specific dollar figures are deliberately not stated here, since the verified pool gives none. The quotation is from the 2006 cross-examination and postdates this stop by four and a half years.
stops.campa: Enron announces a large quarterly loss and heavy charges, and discloses a reduction in shareholders' equity tied to the related-party partnerships its own chief financial officer had been running on the side. The disclosure reconciles to nothing already filed. A trading house of this kind holds nothing but the willingness of the people on the other side of its trades, and from this date the company's statements stop being believed. The credit agencies begin the downgrades. The counterparties begin to withdraw.
stops.quote: I think we're now getting into form over substance, Mr. Hueston.
stops.quote_source: Kenneth Lay, criminal trial testimony under cross-examination, 2006, Famous Trials archive
suggested_refs: Enron's third-quarter 2001 announcement and the SEC inquiry that followed it

stops.name: Southern District of New York, Manhattan: Chapter 11
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia. Coordinates approximate the Manhattan federal courthouse district; the exact filing courthouse address was not itemized in any source reached, so the pin marks the venue city rather than a confirmed building. The quotation is 2006 trial testimony looking back on this day.
stops.campa: Enron files for protection under Chapter 11 in the Southern District of New York, the largest corporate bankruptcy in the country's history to that date. Eleven months earlier it had reported revenue of nearly one hundred and one billion dollars. Lay is in Houston, chairman and chief executive of a corporation now in the hands of a court, and he will hold both titles for seven more weeks. The petition itself is filed in Manhattan, sixteen hundred miles from the building the company was run out of.
stops.quote: I think the most painful thing in my life was watching Enron finally have to go into bankruptcy.
stops.quote_source: Kenneth Lay, criminal trial testimony, 2006, quoted in CBS News, 'Prosecutor: Lay Lays Blame Elsewhere'
suggested_refs: The Enron Chapter 11 petition, Southern District of New York, 2 December 2001
sources: CBS News, 'Prosecutor: Lay Lays Blame Elsewhere'

stops.name: 1400 Smith Street, Houston: he resigns
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Wikipedia gives 23 January 2002 as the end date of Lay's chairman and chief executive tenure. The creditors' committee request is the standard account and is not separately documented in the verified pool. The quotation is from the 2006 cross-examination, where Lay was confronted with alternatives to selling Enron stock back to the company during the 2001 credit-line repayments.
stops.campa: He resigns the chairmanship and the chief executive's office on the twenty-third of January, five months and nine days after taking the job back. He had held the chairmanship for nearly sixteen years, and the company that made his name is being taken apart and sold in pieces. In those last months he had sold Enron stock back to the company against a credit line he kept drawing down, and what else he might have done instead will be put to him under oath in a Houston courtroom. He is fifty-nine years old.
stops.quote: There were other options, Mr. Hueston.
stops.quote_source: Kenneth Lay, criminal trial testimony under cross-examination, 2006, Famous Trials archive
suggested_refs: Lay's 2001 stock sales back to Enron against his personal credit line

segments.name: The Fifth Amendment, the Verdict, and the Abatement

stops.name: Capitol Hill, Washington: he takes the Fifth
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to detail, widely reported as to fact. Lay's February 2002 invocation of the Fifth Amendment before congressional investigators is carried by the dossier's characterization of the hearing record and was not independently refetched from a primary transcript. Neither the committee nor the room is identified in anything reached, and the date is fixed only to the month; the pin is a generic Senate office building point on Capitol Hill.
stops.campa: Called before congressional investigators in February, he appears, is sworn, and on the advice of counsel declines to answer. He had spent a decade in Washington rooms as an expert witness and a welcome guest, and he takes the Fifth in one of them. It is the last thing he says publicly about Enron for four years; the next time he explains himself it is under oath in Houston, to a jury. Which committee called him, and which room he sat in, is not recorded in anything that has been reached.
suggested_refs: The February 2002 congressional hearings into the collapse of Enron
sources: Research dossier chronology of the congressional hearings, not independently refetched

stops.name: Houston: the indictment and the surrender
stops.date_confidence: Attested, with corrections recorded. Wikipedia states that Lay was indicted by a Houston grand jury on 7 July 2004 on eleven counts of securities fraud, wire fraud, and making false and misleading statements; 8 July is the unsealing, the surrender, and the SEC civil filing, and is the date used here. An earlier claim that the July 2004 Houston indictment included bank fraud and false statements to banks is wrong: those were a separate case, originally filed in California and later tried to the bench. The White House response is attested by CBS News of 8 July 2004.
stops.campa: A federal grand jury in Houston indicts him on eleven counts of securities fraud, wire fraud, and false and misleading statements. The indictment is unsealed the next day; he surrenders, is processed, and the Securities and Exchange Commission files its civil action the same afternoon. George W. Bush's press secretary says within hours that it has been quite some time since the president spoke with him, and calls him a supporter in the past. Kenny Boy is retired as a form of address.
suggested_refs: The July 2004 Houston indictment of Kenneth Lay and the parallel SEC civil action
sources: CBS News, 'Bush Edges Away From Kenny Boy,' 8 July 2004

stops.name: Bob Casey Courthouse, Houston: the trial opens
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia: the joint trial of Lay and Skilling began on 30 January 2006 in Houston before U.S. District Judge Sim Lake, who had denied defense motions to move the case out of the city. The courthouse building identity is added from general knowledge of Houston's federal courthouse and carries lower confidence than the trial facts. Coordinates corrected during verification: 515 Rusk Street geocodes to 29.7610, -95.3678.
stops.campa: The joint trial of Lay and Skilling opens before Judge Sim Lake, who has refused the defense motions to move the case out of Houston. The courtroom is a few blocks from the tower the company had its name on. The two men are tried together, on separate charges, in front of one jury drawn from the city the company failed in. The charge against Lay is that he told the public Enron was sound in the weeks when he was being told inside the building that it was not. He is sixty-three years old. Nineteen months have passed since the morning he surrendered.
suggested_refs: The Bob Casey United States Courthouse, 515 Rusk Street, Houston

stops.name: Bob Casey Courthouse, Houston: on the stand
stops.date_confidence: The testimony and the cross-examination by prosecutor John Hueston are attested through the transcript excerpts published by the Famous Trials archive at the University of Missouri-Kansas City and through contemporaneous CBS News and CFO.com reporting. The verified pool gives no dates for his days on the stand; 1 May 2006 is an ordering device placed between the opening of the trial and the verdict. The two sentences quoted are reported together with this wording by CFO.com.
stops.campa: He takes the stand in his own defense, and the prosecutor John Hueston cross-examines him for days: the stock sales, the credit line, the boats, the Aspen houses, the assurances given to employees in the autumn of 2001. He concedes error and concedes nothing else. He is combative on the stand, and the jury watches him be combative for days. Did he make mistakes, Hueston asks him. He is sure he did, Lay answers, and he had to make real-time decisions on the information he had at the time.
stops.quote: Did I make mistakes? I'm sure I did, Mr. Hueston. I had to make real-time decisions based on the information I had at the time.
stops.quote_source: Kenneth Lay, criminal trial testimony, 2006, reported in CFO.com, 'Lay Finishes Testimony,' and CBS News
suggested_refs: The Lay testimony transcript excerpts, Famous Trials archive, famous-trials.com/enron/1803-laytestimony
sources: CBS News, 'Prosecutor: Lay Lays Blame Elsewhere'

stops.name: Bob Casey Courthouse, Houston: the verdict
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia: on 25 May 2006 the jury found Lay guilty on all six counts submitted to it, being conspiracy, two counts of wire fraud and three of securities fraud, and in a separate bench trial Judge Sim Lake found him guilty of one count of bank fraud and three counts of false statements to banks, for ten guilty findings in total. Sentencing had been scheduled for 23 October 2006.
stops.campa: The jury returns guilty on all six counts put to it: conspiracy, two of wire fraud, three of securities fraud. In the separate bench trial on the banking charges, Judge Lake finds him guilty of one count of bank fraud and three of false statements to banks. Ten findings of guilt in a single day. He is sixty-four, and he walks out of the courthouse on his own feet, into a Houston afternoon, still at liberty. Sentencing is set for the twenty-third of October.
stops.quote: I loved Enron very much. I think we built a great company.
stops.quote_source: Kenneth Lay, criminal trial testimony, 2006, quoted in CBS News, 'Prosecutor: Lay Lays Blame Elsewhere'
suggested_refs: The 25 May 2006 jury verdict and the parallel bench findings of Judge Sim Lake
sources: CBS News, 'Prosecutor: Lay Lays Blame Elsewhere'

stops.name: Snowmass, Colorado: the last morning
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. Wikipedia gives Snowmass, Colorado (near Aspen) as the place of the collapse, his wife Linda finding him, and the autopsy findings of severe coronary artery disease with evidence of at least two prior heart attacks and previous stents. The Aspen-area property purchases and sales are a reconstruction, resting on a High Country News piece that returned a 403 error on refetch. Sources describe the residence variously as a rented cabin and as the family's own place; no address is documented. Coordinates approximate the Snowmass area.
stops.campa: Six weeks after the verdict and four months before the sentencing, he is at the family's place in the mountains above Aspen, the country where he and Linda had bought and sold property through the boom years. He is sixty-four and has never spent a night in custody. In the early morning he collapses. His wife finds him and calls for help. The autopsy will find severe coronary artery disease, evidence of at least two earlier heart attacks, and stents already in place from some operation the record does not date.
stops.quote: We could have reduced some living costs, but as I said earlier, we had realized the American dream.
stops.quote_source: Kenneth Lay, criminal trial testimony, 2006, quoted in CBS News, 'Prosecutor: Lay Lays Blame Elsewhere'
suggested_refs: The Lays' Aspen-area property transactions, 1991 to 2002
sources: CBS News, 'Prosecutor: Lay Lays Blame Elsewhere'
High Country News reconstruction, refetch returned 403

stops.name: Aspen Valley Hospital: pronounced dead
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Wikipedia records the death by heart attack, the pronouncement at Aspen Valley Hospital, and the ruling of natural death. The cremation is confirmed only by the Spokesman-Review piece of 15 July 2006, which reports it as the detail that fed the fake-death rumor; the PBS NewsHour page originally cited for the cremation was refetched and contains no mention of it. The Powell rumor, the parody images and the shirt price are all from that Spokesman-Review piece. Coordinates corrected during verification: 401 Castle Creek Road geocodes to 39.19060, -106.83936, reconciling two conflicting figures carried in the research lenses.
stops.campa: He is pronounced dead at Aspen Valley Hospital on Castle Creek Road. The death is ruled natural. The family chooses cremation, and because there is then no body and no grave, the internet decides within ten days that there is no death either: that Colin Powell, in Aspen for an unrelated panel, had handed him false travel documents. Parody images circulate of Lay at the Eiffel Tower and running with the bulls in Spain, and shirts reading Ken Lay Lives sell for fourteen dollars and ninety-nine cents.
suggested_refs: Spokesman-Review, 'Internet alive with theories that Lay not really dead,' 15 July 2006

stops.name: Aspen Chapel: the private funeral
stops.date_confidence: Date attested, venue a reconstruction. Wikipedia states that a private funeral for about two hundred people was held in Aspen four days after his death, which fixes 9 July 2006, and names no building. The identification of Aspen Chapel rests on the dossier chronology alone; the Houston Chronicle and legacy.com coverage naming it returned 403 errors on refetch. Coordinates are Aspen Chapel at 77 Meadowood Drive, 39.19405, -106.84089, reconciling two conflicting figures carried in the research lenses. The absence of any grave, plot or monument is a checked negative finding: even the Handbook of Texas records no burial place or memorial of any kind.
stops.campa: A private funeral is held four days after the death, about two hundred people, in a chapel outside Aspen. The eulogies are of a man of faith and a man wronged. There will be no sentencing in October and no appeal. There is no grave for anyone to visit afterward either: no stone, no plot, no monument anywhere in Texas or Missouri or Colorado with his name cut into it. The reference biographies that record his birth to the day record no burial place at all.
suggested_refs: Aspen Chapel, 77 Meadowood Drive, Aspen, Colorado
sources: Research dossier chronology for the venue name, refetch blocked
Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Lay, Kenneth Lee'

stops.name: First United Methodist Church, Houston: the memorial
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to place and substance by Wikipedia, which places a memorial 'a week after his death' at the First United Methodist Church in Houston. The exact day is not given; 12 July is derived from that phrase and is an ordering choice. The content of the eulogies, including the criticism of the prosecution from the pulpit, is carried by Wikipedia and contemporaneous coverage; no order of service is in the verified pool. The Justice Department's stated intention to pursue further civil litigation against the estate is recorded by the Handbook of Texas.
stops.campa: A week after the death a larger memorial is held at First United Methodist Church on Main Street in Houston, in the downtown he had run a corporation out of for fifteen years. Friends and clergy speak about his faith and his philanthropy, and some of the speakers attack the prosecution from the pulpit. Linda Lay is the widow of a man with ten findings of guilt against him and no sentence. The government has already said it means to go after the estate, and the convictions have not yet been vacated.
suggested_refs: First United Methodist Church, 1320 Main Street, Houston
sources: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Lay, Kenneth Lee'

stops.name: Bob Casey Courthouse, Houston: abatement ab initio
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia: on 17 October 2006 Judge Sim Lake vacated Lay's convictions and dismissed the indictment under the doctrine of abatement ab initio, because he died before sentencing and appellate review. The Handbook of Texas gives the vacatur as November 2006, a discrepancy noted and not resolved. The extinguishing of criminal forfeiture is confirmed by attorney Barry Boss on PBS NewsHour; a specific quotation attributed to him elsewhere did not surface on refetch and is therefore not printed here. Coordinates are the Houston federal courthouse, reconciling two conflicting figures in the research lenses.
stops.campa: Six days before the sentencing that will not happen, Judge Sim Lake vacates every conviction and dismisses the indictment. The doctrine is abatement ab initio: a defendant who dies before his appeal is heard returns to the position he held before the case began. Nothing has been decided about the evidence. The jury's verdict of the twenty-fifth of May stands as history and not as law, criminal forfeiture against the estate is extinguished, and the man goes into the record convicted and never convicted at once.
suggested_refs: The 17 October 2006 order of Judge Sim Lake vacating the convictions under abatement ab initio
sources: PBS NewsHour, 'Death of Kenneth Lay Leaves Questions Unanswered'
Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas, 'Lay, Kenneth Lee'
